{"id": "53:34/q07", "question": "How does this verse fit the surrounding argument?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis falls on the immediate unseen-knowledge question, the preceding recompense promise, or the sūra's broader scriptural argument; Asad's excerpt does not identify its proposed earlier connection.", "positions": [{"id": "53:34/q07/p1", "position": "It leads into 53:35's challenge to the person's claimed knowledge of unseen judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers the al-Walīd report because the next question fits a man buying relief from punishment. Bursevī treats the false transfer belief as the focus. Asad asks how scant giving establishes that judgment will not come. Islahi hears sarcasm toward misers behaving as though they already see Paradise's luxury. Al-Qushayrī's reported hypocrite acts as if he knows his unseen afterlife state."}, {"id": "53:34/q07/p2", "position": "It follows 53:31's promise of recompense with astonishment at a man who misunderstands what God rewards.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the preceding fāʾ frames this response; each person has only what he strives for, whereas this man tries to outsource consequences. He distinguishes the prior turning away as blame from the astonishment introduced by the small gift."}, {"id": "53:34/q07/p3", "position": "It leads from the third section's account of creation to enduring teachings in Moses' and Abraham's scriptures.", "reasons": "Study Quran describes the sūra's third section as a call to reflect on creation before the scriptural transition. Islahi invokes those prophets' teaching and sacrifice against presumed inherited entitlement to Paradise."}, {"id": "53:34/q07/p4", "position": "Its wording returns to an earlier theme in the sūra.", "reasons": "Asad says his rendering of 53:33–34 and its bracketed insertions follow Rāzī; the excerpt ends before naming the earlier verses."}]}
{"id": "53:35/q04", "question": "What unseen matter does the question challenge him to know?", "turns_on": "Which hidden claim his conduct presumes: transferable punishment, future poverty, his reward, the truth of revelation, resurrection, or hidden knowledge more generally. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers the worldly-future reading because 53:38 itself addresses transfer of sins.", "positions": [{"id": "53:35/q04/p1", "position": "Whether another person can bear his sins or punishment for him.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, Elmalılı, and Ibn ʿĀshūr apply the question to his companion's undertaking. Al-Zajjāj as reported by al-Wāḥidī also connects knowing to that undertaking. Al-Zamakhsharī as stated in al-Kashshāf and reported by Abū Ḥayyān asks whether his brother's promise is true. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and Abū Ḥayyān frame it as whether assuming another's burden would benefit him. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī connect the supposed transfer to 53:38; Ibn ʿĀshūr says he paid someone to carry the consequences of leaving Islam."}, {"id": "53:35/q04/p2", "position": "Whether continued giving would exhaust his wealth and leave him poor.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says the miser plainly has no unseen knowledge that his money will run out. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers this future course of worldly life. The Study Quran likewise includes whether his wealth remains safe if he withholds charity."}, {"id": "53:35/q04/p3", "position": "Whether he can know his afterlife condition, punishment, or recompense generally.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutaybah includes the affairs of the Hereafter; Ibn al-Jawzī reports al-Farrāʾ on seeing his afterlife condition and Ibn Qutaybah on hidden afterlife affairs. Abū Ḥayyān reports the afterlife-condition view and al-Zajjāj's view that he sees his sin lifted there. Al-Rāzī defines unseen knowledge as what is hidden from creatures and says direct sight occurs only when faith no longer benefits; al-Qurṭubī includes unseen punishment and afterlife events. Qushayri reports a hypocrite who briefly helps with jihad and then stops, as though he knew his unseen afterlife state."}, {"id": "53:35/q04/p4", "position": "Whether he can foresee that his small gift or earlier deeds suffice for reward.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī asks whether he knows every benefit and harm and what God accepts, so can judge his small donation sufficient. Islahi says misers give little yet presume high rank in the Hereafter; the Study Quran mentions confidence that earlier deeds suffice. Islahi also depicts people acting as though Paradise's luxuries are already visible."}, {"id": "53:35/q04/p5", "position": "Whether he knows that what he heard from the Quran is false.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this possibility. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī also report it; Mujāhid, as reported in al-Durr, identifies the unseen as the Quran and asks whether al-Walīd saw falsehood while visiting the Prophet and Abū Bakr."}, {"id": "53:35/q04/p6", "position": "Whether revelation came to him and authorized his judgment that his conduct was right.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Ālūsī report al-Kalbī's view; Abū Ḥayyān reports it with the nuance that he saw what had been withheld from him as true."}, {"id": "53:35/q04/p7", "position": "Whether he knows there will be no resurrection or recompense.", "reasons": "Muqātil says he would need unseen knowledge that he will not be resurrected to justify persistence in disbelief, comparing 52:41 and 68:47. Al-Māwardī reports the possibility that he knew there is no resurrection and thus expected no recompense."}, {"id": "53:35/q04/p8", "position": "Whether he possesses knowledge of hidden matters as though he could see them.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī states the general question. Al-Rāzī calls the unseen what creatures cannot know; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it hidden realms inferred from evidence but expressed as witnessed. Al-Biqāʿī extends the supposed knowledge to every benefit, harm, and divine acceptance. Qushayri describes the supposed knowledge as knowledge of the truth of the matter."}, {"id": "53:35/q04/p9", "position": "Whether he was informed of the content of Moses' scrolls.", "reasons": "Bursevī gives this alternative as ignorance of what is in Moses' scrolls, meaning the books of the Torah."}]}
{"id": "53:35/q05", "question": "What does yarā mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether seeing the unseen is a figure for knowing it or is treated as direct visual perception; several commentators explicitly allow both.", "positions": [{"id": "53:35/q05/p1", "position": "It denotes knowledge or inward perception.", "reasons": "Sībawayh as reported by al-Naḥḥās glosses it as knowing. Al-Zajjāj, reported also by al-Wāḥidī, illustrates this with a blind person saying he sees Zayd as intelligent. Bursevī and Ibn al-Shaykh use 'knows'; al-Ālūsī calls this the more immediate sense. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Zajjāj allow this meaning alongside sight. Qushayri explains the question whether he sees as whether he knows the truth of the matter."}, {"id": "53:35/q05/p2", "position": "It denotes actual sight of what is hidden from others.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Ālūsī allow physical sight. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the verb visually with the unseen as its omitted object. Al-Rāzī says such direct sight would only be available when faith no longer benefits."}]}
{"id": "53:35/q09", "question": "Whom does the question address?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding relative expression names the man in a particular report or presents a representative figure; Islahi disputes the report's chain and fit.", "positions": [{"id": "53:35/q09/p1", "position": "It addresses the person who turned away in the preceding passage, portrayed as a miser.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the pronouns refer to that person and the question repudiates him. Ibn Kathīr and Islahi read the conduct as withholding gifts; the Study Quran calls him the man who stopped giving charity."}, {"id": "53:35/q09/p2", "position": "It concerns al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah in a reported incident.", "reasons": "Islahi reports exegetes' identification of this Quraysh chief and his abandoned plan to embrace Islam. Mujāhid's report in al-Durr places al-Walīd with the Prophet and Abū Bakr. Islahi objects that the report lacks a sound chain and that the generic relative expression has been treated as a proper name; Kuran Yolu likewise calls the episode reports unreliable and discordant with Qur'anic principles."}, {"id": "53:35/q09/p3", "position": "It is a representative miserly idolater, depicting a wider group.", "reasons": "Islahi says al-ladhī and al can introduce a parable of a group's collective character, comparing the woman unravelling her thread in 16:92. He describes Arabs who refuse to spend yet expect Paradise through alleged deities and racial superiority; al-Walīd, Abū Jahl, and other wealthy Quraysh can recognize themselves in it."}, {"id": "53:35/q09/p4", "position": "A hypocrite who briefly helps with jihad and then stops.", "reasons": "Qushayri reports this identification of the person."}]}
{"id": "53:35/q10", "question": "What incident is reported behind the rebuke?", "turns_on": "The reports differ over the actor and transaction, and Islahi and Kuran Yolu question the reliability or relevance of the reported episode.", "positions": [{"id": "53:35/q10/p1", "position": "Al-Walīd abandoned conversion after someone promised to shield him from the Hereafter for payment, of which he paid only part.", "reasons": "Islahi recounts the exegetes' report. He objects that it has no sound chain, its link to the verses is unclear, and the Quran is not rebuking al-Walīd for breaking a promise. Kuran Yolu says such episode reports are unreliable and their details sit uneasily with Qur'anic principles."}, {"id": "53:35/q10/p2", "position": "A new Muslim feared God, paid an opponent offering relief from all punishment, bargained after paying a little, and documented the deal.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports this account from Ibn Zayd."}, {"id": "53:35/q10/p3", "

{"id": "53:35/q13", "question": "What does the rebuking question expose?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either unwarranted private knowledge and self-sufficiency or the ironic confidence of those claiming heavenly status.", "positions": [{"id": "53:35/q13/p1", "position": "It exposes his ignorance, need for guidance, and unjustified confidence in unseen judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls turning away ugly while hidden matters still require a guide; only direct sight at a time when faith no longer helps could excuse it. His alternative says the man thinks his judgment sufficient without guide or warner. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the verse a repudiation of his mistaken confidence, and the Study Quran extends the criticism to people acting as if they know better than God, comparing 52:41 and 68:47. Qushayri's reported hypocrite stops helping with jihad as though he knew his unseen afterlife state."}, {"id": "53:35/q13/p2", "position": "It uses sarcastic irony toward misers who presume Paradise is already visible to them.", "reasons": "Islahi contrasts their grudging gifts with their confidence in Paradise's luxuries; he also criticizes the assumption that Abrahamic or Mosaic descent guarantees Paradise instead of attending to those prophets' teachings and sacrifices."}]}
{"id": "53:36/q01", "question": "What does 'am lam yunabba' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:36/q01/p1", "position": "Rather, has he not been told or informed?", "reasons": "Wahidi al-Basit and Nasafi gloss yunabba as being informed; Abu Hayyan and Alusi explain am as 'rather'; Bursevi frames it as the possibility that he never heard the scriptural teaching. Farra glosses the full phrase أم لم ينبأ as ألم ينبأ, a direct 'has he not been informed?' Qushayri expresses the question as whether the addressee has heard the scriptural teaching."}]}
{"id": "53:36/q03", "question": "What rebuke does the question convey?", "turns_on": "The notes differ in whether they stress the failed excuse of ignorance or the obligation to consult earlier revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "53:36/q03/p1", "position": "The person turning away cannot claim complete ignorance of the earlier teaching.", "reasons": "Razi says one who fully knows needs no instruction and one wholly unaware, like a sleeper, is not addressed; neither condition excuses this person. Bursevi states the question as whether he has never been told. Qushayri frames the question as whether the unbeliever has heard the teaching in Moses' and Abraham's scriptures."}, {"id": "53:36/q03/p2", "position": "If he rejects Muhammad, he should seek the earlier messengers' teaching on fearing God and escaping punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls this second interrogative another rebuke."}]}
{"id": "53:36/q04", "question": "Whom does the question address?", "turns_on": "Razi makes the audience depend on whether bima means the message's shared teachings or the actual contents received by a scriptured community.", "positions": [{"id": "53:36/q04/p1", "position": "It addresses Quraysh primarily and the People of the Book secondarily.", "reasons": "Islahi says Quraysh claimed Abraham as ancestor and religious leader, while the People of the Book claimed Moses and Abraham."}, {"id": "53:36/q04/p2", "position": "It can address both idolaters and the People of the Book.", "reasons": "Razi says the Prophet proclaimed teachings such as monotheism and resurrection found in Moses' scrolls, so both audiences heard their substance."}, {"id": "53:36/q04/p3", "position": "It specifically addresses the People of the Book.", "reasons": "On Razi's alternative, bima points to the scriptures' actual contents, received by that community; he also proposes that the person who ceased giving God's rights when Muhammad came may have possessed a book."}, {"id": "53:36/q04/p4", "position": "It addresses the unbeliever.", "reasons": "Qushayri explicitly identifies the person asked whether he has heard the scriptural teaching as the unbeliever."}]}
{"id": "53:36/q14", "question": "What did Abraham fulfill in the following description?", "turns_on": "The reports variously specify comprehensive obedience, particular acts of worship, or the rule of individual liability as the fulfillment.", "positions": [{"id": "53:36/q14/p1", "position": "He fully discharged God's commands, trials, vows, and duty of servitude.", "reasons": "Zajjaj lists his resolve to sacrifice his son, endurance of his people's hostility and the fire, and circumcision. Mawrdi reports Ibn Abbas on obedience, Hasan on every command and vow, and trials of sacrifice, fire, and being called a liar. Ibn Kathir reports Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Thawri that he fulfilled every command. Tabrisi glosses waffa as completing his commands; Tabatabai says he perfectly discharged servitude and cites the completed trials of 2:124. Thalabi includes conveying God's message and the rule against another's burden. Qushayri specifies that Abraham fulfilled what was required of him concerning himself, his wealth, and his child."}, {"id": "53:36/q14/p2", "position": "He fulfilled each day's worship with four midmorning rakas.", "reasons": "Mawrdi reports this from the Prophet through Abu Umama."}, {"id": "53:36/q14/p3", "position": "He fulfilled morning and evening glorification.", "reasons": "Mawrdi reports through Anas and his father that Abraham recited the glorification verse at both times, citing 30:17."}, {"id": "53:36/q14/p4", "position": "He established the principle that no one bears a relative's offense.", "reasons": "Mawrdi reports al-Hudhayl that Abraham opposed the earlier practice of charging a person with a child's or parent's offense, connecting this to 53:38; Thalabi includes this principle in his mission."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q04", "question": "What does سَعَىٰ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether saʿy is work, intention, causal contribution, or relinquished effort.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q04/p1", "position": "It denotes one's work, deeds, or earning.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī says deeds; al-Baghawī cites 92:4. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says earning. Bursevī and al-Rāghib define literal brisk walking slower than running, extended to earnest effort in good or evil; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the extension metaphor or metonymy. Al-Rāzī says seeking an object would normally take fīhi. Ibn Zayd glosses the striving mentioned in 92:4 as people's deeds."}, {"id": "53:39/q04/p2", "position": "It means what the person intends.", "reasons": "Al-Warrāq cites resurrection according to intention. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ distinguishes seeking God's pleasure from seeking reward. Asad cites a widely transmitted intention hadith and includes deliberate omissions and expressed belief in conscious action."}, {"id": "53:39/q04/p3", "position": "One's striving includes one's causal contribution to another's deed.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī names a call to faith; Ibn al-Zāghūnī names kin, child, friend and service to religion; al-Biqāʿī and Islāḥī include ties, teaching, example and financial help."}, {"id": "53:39/q04/p4", "position": "It is the effort one repudiates as one's own.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī says a person has only what they disclaim of their striving."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q07", "question": "What does the verse say a person receives?", "turns_on": "Whether the limit applies to all deeds, a kind of deed, strict entitlement, or material earnings.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q07/p1", "position": "One receives recompense for one's own deeds, good for good and evil for evil.", "reasons": "Muqātil locates it in the Hereafter; Ibn Qutayba and al-Wāḥidī stress preparation for it. Al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq include good and evil; al-Rāzī reports this as well known. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī contrasts enduring deeds with wealth, children and status lost at death. Al-Ṭabarī explicitly says recompense covers good and bad deeds alike."}, {"id": "53:39/q07/p2", "position": "The apparent point concerns benefits from good deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite lām for benefit rather than ʿalā for liability. Al-Rāzī says v. 41's full recompense suits good while evil can be matched, reduced or forgiven."}, {"id": "53:39/q07/p3", "position": "The restriction may concern evil deeds specifically.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites a sound Muslim report: an unperformed good intention is credited, accomplished good multiplied up to seven hundred, and accomplished evil counted once."}, {"id": "53:39/q07/p4", "position": "Only one's own earned deed is owed; more can come by divine grace.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl reconciles the verse with multiplication, citing 2:261 or 2:245; al-Thaʿlabī tells Ibn Ṭāhir's questions about Cain and God's daily act and recounts al-Ḥusayn's reply and the other view of Cain's regret. Ibn ʿAṭiyya names intercession, relatives, multiplication and forgiveness. Al-Qurṭubī cites tenfold to seven-hundredfold and Abū Hurayra's two-millionfold report. Al-Rāzī says even tenfold reward is sought in hoping for God's promise, citing 6:160."}, {"id": "53:39/q07/p5", "position": "Another's gift can benefit someone without becoming that person's earned entitlement.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī compares children admitted to Paradise without deeds of their own. Elmalılı distinguishes true ownership from gifts and commanded cooperation. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says bodily and financial good can benefit both doer and recipient, citing Saʿd's charity for his mother."}, {"id": "53:39/q07/p6", "position": "The verse denies reliance on another's work.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr lists this among harmonizations with reports of others' good deeds."}, {"id": "53:39/q07/p7", "position": "Earnings should be proportional to one's labor.", "reasons": "Some readers infer material earnings proportionate to labor; Islāḥī rejects this as unrelated to the verse's context."}, {"id": "53:39/q0

7/p8", "position": "Worldly provision tests gratitude and patience; the Hereafter rewards earned deeds.", "reasons": "Islāḥī distinguishes the distribution of worldly provision from final reward and punishment; Kur'an Yolu affirms honest labor's value before God and places voluntary choice within a test whose full secrets exceed human knowledge."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q08", "question": "Can another person's deed benefit someone under this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether entitlement, causal connection, proxy intention, or limited scope governs others' deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q08/p1", "position": "Another's deed gives no earned reward apart from one's own effort.", "reasons": "The preceding ban on bearing another's burden is parallel, according to al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Study Quran. Islāḥī cites 2:134, Noah's son, Abraham's father, Lot's wife and Pharaoh's wife in 66:11 against automatic inherited reward. Al-Ṭabarī states that no worker receives another's reward or punishment."}, {"id": "53:39/q08/p2", "position": "Another's deed can count as one's own through faith or causal effort.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Ālūsī and Ebussuud require faith, good conduct or a causal role. Al-Ālūsī recounts al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil's vow of a hundred camels, Hishām's fifty sacrifices and the Prophet's conditional statement about monotheism. Ibn Kathīr treats endowment, useful teaching and a child's prayer as traces of one's efforts, citing 36:12 and a hadith that a child is one's earning. Islāḥī adds ties of faith, teaching and aid."}, {"id": "53:39/q08/p3", "position": "Another's deed can count through a proxy intending it for the recipient.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī's second answer contrasts self-directed deeds with work for the deceased. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī treat the performer as agent; al-Ālūsī notes figurative usage."}, {"id": "53:39/q08/p4", "position": "Believers can receive others' efforts because the restriction concerns unbelievers.", "reasons": "Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas is transmitted by these sources."}, {"id": "53:39/q08/p5", "position": "Muslims can benefit from others because the rule concerned Abraham's and Moses's peoples.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima's account is cited repeatedly; Ibn ʿĀshūr treats acceptance of another's deed as a special concession."}, {"id": "53:39/q08/p6", "position": "An unbeliever's good is paid in worldly life, leaving none for the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī recount ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy's shirt for al-ʿAbbās and the Prophet's reciprocal shroud."}, {"id": "53:39/q08/p7", "position": "Reports show benefit through charity, pilgrimage, prayer, or continuing deeds.", "reasons": "They include Saʿd's charity for his mother, a dead father's or sister's Hajj, a child's Hajj, and posthumous prayer. Al-Qurṭubī calls charity undisputed, Bursevī cites many reports, and an unnamed report in al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says even a nāṣib's burden can be lightened by a gifted deed."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q09", "question": "Has this rule been abrogated or qualified?", "turns_on": "Whether 52:21 alters a factual report, qualifies scope, or leaves the rule intact.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q09/p1", "position": "It was abrogated for this community by 52:21.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is cited, including through al-Wālibī: children enter Paradise and rise by parental righteousness. Al-Qurṭubī adds family intercession and 4:11; Bursevī mentions it too. Al-Durr calls 52:21 a qualification; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports ʿIkrima's earlier-law view. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies 52:21, which joins believing descendants to righteous forebears, as the abrogating verse."}, {"id": "53:39/q09/p2", "position": "It remains definitive; a report of fact cannot be abrogated.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn al-Jawzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Rāzī and Elmalılı challenge attribution or naskh's conditions. The majority holds the rule in force. Elmalılı says 52:21 is consistent and also pledges each person to earnings. Al-Ālūsī transmits Abū Ḥayyān's objection that a report, not a command, cannot be abrogated."}, {"id": "53:39/q09/p3", "position": "It can be specified for Muslims without being abrogated.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says an earlier-scripture report may be qualified. Ibn ʿĀshūr lists exception, specification or abrogation among harmonizations."}, {"id": "53:39/q09/p4", "position": "Proxy worship depends on whether the rule remains operative.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī bar it absent abrogation, except for proven cases such as Hajj; the reported abrogation removes that bar."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q10", "question": "How does the verse connect to its surroundings and earlier scriptures?", "turns_on": "Which nearby or intertextual frame explains the personal-accountability statement.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q10/p1", "position": "It belongs to the teachings in Abraham's and Moses's scrolls.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Nasafī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Study Quran connect it to 53:36–37; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī counts seventeen verses. Islāḥī contrasts their teachings and sacrifices with inherited claims."}, {"id": "53:39/q10/p2", "position": "It completes the rule that no soul bears another's burden.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say another's good cannot simply transfer any more than their sins; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it blocks an inference that only sins are personal. Al-Rāzī links Abraham's failed prayer for his father with both rules; he says the no-burden rule is the most apparent scroll content, though the scrolls hold more."}, {"id": "53:39/q10/p3", "position": "It is compared with verses about varied effort, individual earnings and enduring traces.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī cites 92:4; Elmalılı cites 2:286 and 52:21. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī connects 36:12, 4:9 and 8:37 to traces of acts and descendants; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ uses an echo of this verse. Ibn Zayd reads the striving of 92:4 as people's deeds."}, {"id": "53:39/q10/p4", "position": "It rebukes claims to ancestral rank without personal effort.", "reasons": "Islāḥī says people boasting of Abraham or Moses while withholding charity should heed these prophets' teaching."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q15", "question": "How is striving understood on the spiritual path?", "turns_on": "Whether the spiritual fruit is earned, divinely granted, or beyond ordinary striving.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q15/p1", "position": "Effort belongs to wayfaring; realization depends on divine carrying or attraction.", "reasons": "Al-Naṣrābādhī contrasts the paths of wayfaring and Reality, seeing the kingdom and seeing the King, with poems about the rare traveler and the beloved. Bursevī cites Jāmī: years of exertion cannot arrive without divine attraction. He says effort and attraction meet in God and many paths converge."}, {"id": "53:39/q15/p2", "position": "Striving, its visibility, recompense, annihilation, and renewed life mark successive stations.", "reasons": "Al-Warrāq maps vv. 39–43 to beginner, middle, end, loss of individual will, and second arising. Bursevī adds witnessing, subsistence, bodily nourishment and delayed lawful provision."}, {"id": "53:39/q15/p3", "position": "Pure deeds earn Paradise, while vision and nearness are gifts to the spirit.", "reasons": "Al-Baqlī says deeds must lack ostentation; Paradise levels are earned, but unveiling, witness and intimacy come by God's grace."}, {"id": "53:39/q15/p4", "position": "Reward and punishment follow settled dispositions; spiritual returns differ.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says repeated acts shape dispositions, though divine decree governs immediate fortunes; he names bodily resurrection, return to primordial heart and return to gifted Real existence after annihilation, only the first universal."}, {"id": "53:39/q15/p5", "position": "Self-knowledge and restraint of desire safeguard effort.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā al-Hāshimī says most striving follows desires."}, {"id": "53:39/q15/p6", "position": "Striving has distinct ends: worldly pursuit loses, seeking Paradise profits, self-discipline wins God's approval, and spiritual aspiration receives God's thanks and guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī distinguishes these four kinds of striving and their outcomes."}, {"id": "53:39/q15/p7", "position": "A sinner's striving for forgiveness and remorse over a darkened record leads to reward and nearness to God.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says the repentant sinner receives reward, nearness, honor, and intimacy from God."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q05", "question": "What time does سوف mark?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q05/p1", "position": "It marks a future event, usually understood as distant.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives the usual force of سوف. Elmalılı says the effort's fruit need not appear immediately, yet the effort is not lost. Qushayrī says the attentive servant sees his effort thanked both in this life and in the next."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q16", "question": "How do the neighboring statements address the fears and hopes of righteous people and sinners?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q16/p1", "position": "The wording leaves sinners hope of forgiveness and reassures the righteous about what they earn.", "reasons": "Rāzī says bearing no other's burden does not exclude God's forgiving one's own burden. For the righteous, 'only what he strives for' affirms receipt of what is earned; phrasing it as 'not what he did not strive for' would not. This balance expresses mercy preceding wrath. Qushayrī says a sinner who seeks forgiveness and regrets the darkening of his record receives reward, nearness, honor, and intimacy from God."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q17", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from a person seeing their striving?", "turns_on": "Whether seeing effort exposes dependence on grace, removes self-credit, or discloses stages of the inward path.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q17/p1", "position": "One sees on

e's striving is unfit for God and survives only through divine grace.", "reasons": "Tustarī and Sahl say the servant learns what the striving merits; without the Lord's grace, it would perish or cause the servant to perish."}, {"id": "53:40/q17/p2", "position": "Striving is not a means of earning reward.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī says this of the Prophet's striving in al-Sulamī, and Bursevī reports the principle without that limitation."}, {"id": "53:40/q17/p3", "position": "Recognition of a work's defects makes one dislike credit for it.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥafṣ says one disowns attribution of deficient work to oneself and dislikes being recalled for it."}, {"id": "53:40/q17/p4", "position": "The path of striving moves through beginning, middle, and end, with distinct gifts at the end.", "reasons": "Al-Warrāq says annihilation is rewarded with witnessing and subsistence with bodily nurture, including lawful provisions deferred on the path."}, {"id": "53:40/q17/p5", "position": "Striving has four inward levels, each with its own result.", "reasons": "Bursevī describes the ego's purification from violations and natural conformity, yielding gardens; {"id": "53:42/q01", "question": "How is the opening clause read and connected to the earlier scriptures?", "turns_on": "Whether the hamza is opened, coordinating the clause with the earlier anna, or broken with kasra to begin a new sentence.", "positions": [{"id": "53:42/q01/p1", "position": "With fatḥa on anna, this clause continues the statements in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf says the fatḥa makes all these clauses part of the scriptures; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it the majority reading and coordinates it with the understood anna of verse 38. Al-Razi calls it the common reading. Al-Samin says the coordinated hamzas share it. Al-Nasafi, al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Jawzi reporting al-Zajjaj, Ibn Ashur, and Study Quran place the statements in those scrolls; Ibn Ashur says it has the syntactic position of verse 40 and notes Abraham's going to his Lord in 37:99 as a possible parallel. Study Quran says verses 42–50 except 46 begin wa anna; its introduction places these perennial truths after the call to reflect on creation. Islahi says Abraham's and Moses' real teachings and sacrifices challenge those assuming descent from them ensures Paradise. Al-Farra says readers use fatḥa; through al-Aʿmash from Ibrahim he reports that ʿAlqama read fatḥa in both al-Najm and al-Jinn (72:3)."}, {"id": "53:42/q01/p2", "position": "With kasra on inna, this and following clauses begin independent statements outside the earlier scriptures' contents.", "reasons": "Abu al-Sammal Qanab is named by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Samin as reading kasra here and onward. Al-Kashshaf, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Alusi, and Study Quran explain the break; Study Quran gives the independent sense as 'truly,' 'surely,' or 'verily.' Al-Farra judges kasra sound when the clause starts a new sentence."}]}
{"id": "53:42/q06", "question": "What ultimately ends with the Lord?", "turns_on": "The notes dispute whether the unrestricted 'ending' denotes bodily return, final outcomes, hopes, the limit of thought, causal explanation, or all kinds of ending; al-Tabatabai argues against restricting its scope.", "positions": [{"id": "53:42/q06/p1", "position": "Creatures return to God after death or at resurrection for judgment and recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas, al-Thaʿlabi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, and others add recompense for good and bad deeds; al-Wahidi calls this the exegetes' interpretation. Ibn ʿAtiyya calls it the gathering and destination after death, relative to worldly life. Al-Razi calls resurrection the well-known interpretation and says it answers when the prior recompense occurs: gratitude is rewarded and ingratitude punished. Al-Kashshaf cites 35:18; al-Nasafi cites 3:28. Ibn Kathir specifies Judgment Day, Study Quran says all then stand before God, and al-Alusi says no other being has an independent or shared part in their return. Al-Bursevi cites 42:53 and says beginning and end are in God. Al-Biqai includes bodily resurrection and the return of deeds; Elmalili includes full recompense and calls God First and Last. Islahi says no one can evade accountability by appealing to another and God's decisions are final. Kuranyolu says judgment gives full recompense without the slightest injustice, while grace and forgiveness remain God's choice and believers should hope without complacency. Al-Tabatabai rejects making this the only meaning as too narrow."}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p2", "position": "The ultimate destination is specifically God's reckoning, reward in Paradise, or punishment in Hell, where earthly action ends.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya contrasts Paradise or Hell as the absolute endpoint with the postmortem gathering relative to worldly life, and posits an omitted genitive: the end of God's mercy or punishment. Al-Tabrisi names divine reward and punishment where deeds cease; Ibn Kathir reports Muʿadh ibn Jabal saying the return ends in Paradise or Fire. Al-Alusi reports reckonings, Paradise, and Fire as commentators' glosses. Study Quran cites 13:35 for the Garden of the reverent versus the Fire of disbelievers. Al-Tabatabai rejects restriction to reward and punishment or reckoning as unsupported narrowing."}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p3", "position": "All beneficence begins with God and all hopes, or security, finally end with Him.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi and al-Baghawi report beneficence and hopes; al-Qurtubi has favor and security. Al-Jishumi lists grace and hopes among reported senses."}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p4", "position": "Human inquiry and thought reach their limit at God, whose essence and attributes cannot be encompassed.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi permits reasoning about created things but says divine knowledge, essence, and modality elude comprehension. Al-Jishumi reports the limit of thought; al-Alusi applies it to divine essence and attributes. Reports from Ubayy, Anas, Abu Hurayra, Ibn Abbas, and Abu Dharr support stopping or turning to creation, detailed in the reflection question. Al-Razi interprets Ubayy's and Anas's reports as reaching the uncaused necessary existent; he says reflection from outward objects stops at God. Al-Tabatabai rejects making the limit of thought the verse's only sense, while treating the Imam al-Sadiq's instruction as an expanded application of 'ending.'"}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p5", "position": "All beings, their effects, governance, deeds, knowledge, hopes, and every other ending depend on God, their origin as well as final end.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai reads the unrestricted infinitive noun absolutely: God creates beings and their relations, directly or through causes, and all governance returns to Him; he cites 39:62–63 and 7:54. Al-Biqai includes bodily return and deeds, knowledge, hopes, affairs, place, and time. Asad includes the universe's beginning and end in time and space, God as source and goal. Bursevi cites 42:53 for affairs returning to God because there is no other deity. Al-Husayn's explanation of tawhid, transmitted by al-Sulami and Bursevi, says contingent effects arise from God, return to Him, and vanish while their cause remains; al-Sulami cites 'He is the First' in 57:3. Al-Razi reads the generic article as every terminus belonging to its origin. Al-Qushayri describes creation from God as the beginning and return to Him as the end."}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p6", "position": "The chain of causes and rational inquiry ends at God as the uncaused Necessary Being and source of existence.", "reasons": "Al-Razi argues contingent things require causes and an explanatory chain cannot finish with another contingent thing. He takes Ubayy's and Anas's stop-at-God reports in this sense. He warns that extending the same reading to every return or ascent verse, such as 35:10, lacks apparent support in some cases though it is clear here. Study Quran reports this understanding from R. Al-Jishumi mentions God as final judge among several reported views, distinct from the causal proof."}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p7", "position": "All knowledge ultimately ends with the Lord.", "reasons": "Muqatil states the epistemic endpoint without further argument."}]}
{"id": "53:42/q07", "question": "What guidance about contemplating God is drawn from the verse and its reports?", "turns_on": "Whether the transmitted prohibitions express the verse's whole sense or an application directed especially to those unready for difficult inquiry.", "positions": [{"id": "53:42/q07/p1", "position": "Stop speculation about God Himself and reflect on His creation instead.", "reasons": "Ubayy ibn Kaʿb's Prophetic report is transmitted by al-Thaʿlabi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, al-Biqai, al-Durr, and a

l-Alusi; some explicitly give no grading. Anas or Sufyan al-Thawri transmit 'when the Lord is mentioned, stop.' Abu Hurayra, Ibn Abbas, and Abu Dharr transmit the creation-versus-Creator instruction because thought cannot encompass Him, with Abu Dharr warning of ruin. Al-Thaʿlabi's Abu Hurayra report describes layers of earth, heavens, and a sea in the seventh heaven. Ibn Kathir says the wording of Abu Hurayra's raised report is not preserved; he cites a sound Satanic-question hadith requiring refuge and stopping, and a Sunan report including an angel's three-hundred-year earlobe-to-shoulder distance. Al-Durr transmits Yunus ibn Maysara's account of the companions discussing God's greatness and the Prophet redirecting them, and a Kufa imam's report of reflection on the sun and a radiant western land inhabited by beings unaware whether Adam or Iblis was created. Al-Biqai adds Ibn Abbas's inability-to-grasp-God's-measure report. Imam al-Sadiq applies the verse to stopping speech when it reaches God. Imam al-Baqir warns Ziyad that forbidden disputation brings doubt, void deeds, and confusion, or wandering in a variant. Al-Wahidi specifies that divine knowledge, essence, and modality cannot be comprehended; al-Alusi says most transmitted proofs indicate the essence cannot be known in its full reality. Al-Jishumi gives no grading for the creation report. Al-Qushayri transmits an unnamed saying to fall silent when speech reaches God. Al-Itqan reports al-Baghawi explicitly comparing Ubayy's no-contemplation explanation with the instruction to reflect on God's creatures rather than His essence."}, {"id": "53:42/q07/p2", "position": "The warning especially guides people unprepared for difficult rational inquiry; the stop-at-God report is an expanded application of 'ending.'", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai says difficult speculation risks lasting ruin for such people, and interprets Imam al-Sadiq's instruction as a broader application rather than limiting the verse's entire meaning. {"id": "53:42/q11", "question": "How is ending with God understood inwardly?", "turns_on": "These reports develop different experiential images of reaching God: transformed will, converging paths, vanished effects, and boundless reality.", "positions": [{"id": "53:42/q11/p1", "position": "Knowing God's lordship removes temptation and leaves the servant willing only what God chooses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtaʾ, reported by al-Sulami, says every trial turns away when a servant reaches that knowledge. Bursevi reports his formulation that whoever begins from God ends with Him and loses any will apart from God's choice."}, {"id": "53:42/q11/p2", "position": "All paths to God converge in one end, despite the number of paths matching creatures' breaths.", "reasons": "Bursevi says their unity lies in the end and God brings the seeker after death to the aspiration sought."}, {"id": "53:42/q11/p3", "position": "Contingent things begin and end in God, then disappear while their abiding cause remains.", "reasons": "Al-Husayn defines tawhid through God's encompassing presence in al-Sulami's account, citing 'He is the First' (57:3); Bursevi reports his cause-and-effect formulation."}, {"id": "53:42/q11/p4", "position": "God's boundlessness dwarfs all other existences as a sea dwarfs streams and seas.", "reasons": "Bursevi quotes Rumi's poetic comparison."}, {"id": "53:42/q11/p5", "position": "After knowing God, the servant receives further divine kindnesses, including gifts, fulfilled hopes, and spiritual states.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri reports this as an unnamed saying about what remains after the servant reaches knowledge of God."}]}
{"id": "70:22/q02", "question": "From what are the worshippers excepted?", "turns_on": "Whether the exception is stated only against the immediate human traits or also against their final outcome.", "positions": [{"id": "70:22/q02/p1", "position": "They are exempt from the human tendency to panic in adversity and withhold good in prosperity.", "reasons": "Muqatil names anxiety and miserliness. Sahl, as reported by Sulami, contrasts despair in poverty and withholding in wealth with enabled worshippers. Samarrai explicitly applies the exception to both sides of haluʿ in 70:20–21. Abu Hayyan contrasts patience in hardship and the noble traits that follow. Biqai says prayer restrains this nature so neither distress nor withholding becomes extreme; the worshippers seek God's pleasure. Bursevi calls this a transformation of blameworthy traits. Baydawi and Alusi describe obedience, care for others, belief in judgment, fear of punishment, restrained desire, and preference for the hereafter as the opposing qualities. Tabatabai says prayer heads the good works because of its strong effect against greed, citing 29:45 for its restraint of shameful conduct and wrongdoing. Kuranyolu connects the cure to responsibility rooted in afterlife belief, worship, and constructive conduct. Study Quran's R and Z prefer the implication that the condemned traits describe humanity broadly because praying people are exempted. Al-Tabatabai cites this exception from anxiety in hardship and withholding in prosperity as evidence of prayer's importance against Satan's effects in his discussion of 5:91."}, {"id": "70:22/q02/p2", "position": "Believing worshippers are also spared the torment and evil end and honored in gardens.", "reasons": "Elmalili ties the exception to the following virtues and the final promise of honor in gardens. Samarrai connects their deliverance from Hell's punishment to their turning toward obedience and truth, in contrast to those whom Hell calls for turning away."}]}
{"id": "74:11/q04", "question": "What does 'alone' describe and mean here?", "turns_on": "The grammatical attachment of the circumstantial accusative to God, the created person, or the speaker's pronoun; whether an epithet is recalled, mocked, or understood as blame.", "positions": [{"id": "74:11/q04/p1", "position": "The man was created alone, initially without wealth, children, or support.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Mujāhid and many others specify no wealth or sons; Wāḥidī's majority also says no wife. Tabarī, Thaʿlabī, Bagha wī and others put him in his mother's womb. Qushayrī says without a supporter; Iṣlāḥī adds status, companions and confidants; Biqāʿī says from nothing, through stages, with no property. Grammatically waḥīdan is the circumstantial accusative of the created man, the relative man, or its omitted object, as Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Nasafī, Samīn and Ibn ʿĀshūr explain; Naḥḥās and Zajjāj identify a circumstantial accusative. Abū Ḥayyān calls this the apparent parse; Ibn ʿAtiyya prefers it if the nickname is unproved. Kashshāf, Rāzī, Elmalılı and Iṣlāḥī compare the solitary first creation at 6:94. God later gave him wealth and sons, intensifying his ingratitude; Muqātil, Qatāda, Māwardī, Kashshāf, Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr and others make that contrast. Al-Farrāʾ calls the reading that the man was created without wealth or sons more comprehensive than the reading that God created him alone."}, {"id": "74:11/q04/p2", "position": "God alone created the man, without any partner in creation.", "reasons": "Zajjāj gives this as the other referent of the circumstantial accusative. Wāḥidī attributes the construction to al-Farrāʾ, al-Kisāʾī and Zajjāj: God knows the man and has power over him. Kashshāf, Rāzī, Samīn, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī add that the sole Creator can own, avenge or destroy him without help. Biqāʿī draws a contrast with the man's shirk. Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers this parse, because God alone created and managed the man and can be entrusted with him. Elmalılı and Asad emphasize the Creator's uniqueness."}, {"id": "74:11/q04/p3", "position": "God is alone with the man to avenge and punish him.", "reasons": "Waḥīdan is circumstantial from the first-person object of dharnī, as Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī and Samīn explain. Mujāhid, cited by Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī, says God suffices as the man's avenger; Kashshāf says no other avenger is needed. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this parse without preferring it."}, {"id": "74:11/q04/p4", "position": "It alludes, often derisively, to al-Walīd's epithet 'the Unique One' or his boast of being without equal.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says he was called al-Waḥīd; ʿAṭāʾ reports his boast 'unique son of the unique,' unequaled among Arabs. Reports explain the title by unmatched wealth, sons, rank and leadership; Ibn ʿĀshūr says he was older than Abū Jahl and Abū Sufyān. Al-Qummī instead says he claimed sole responsibility for one year's Kaʿba covering while Quraysh shared the next. Kashshāf says the title may postdate the verse; otherwise the verse mocks worldly distinction by recalling destitution. Rāzī and Samīn parse it as an accusative of disparagement, with Ṭabāṭabāʾī reporting an implied 'I condemn.' Ibn ʿĀshūr says the wording shifts from his boast to dependence at birth, citing 16:78. Wāḥidī rejects the nickname as the intended sense because God would appear to affirm a false boast; Ibn ʿAtiyya finds its report unproved. Rāzī answers that a proper name need not assert its quality, or means unique in his own estimation, citing 44:49; Qurṭubī likewise says a boast can be repeated without endorsement."}, {"id": "74:11/q04/p5", "position": "It disparages him as uniquely wicked, lowly, or insignificant.", "reasons": "Rāzī says uniqueness need not denote rank: it can mark unbelief, vileness and lowliness. Bayḍāwī, Samīn, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursawī and Ālūsī similarly turn the boast into blame. Abū Ḥayyān cites the proper-name response to an objection over insult; Bursawī cites 44:49."}, {"id": "74:11/q04/p6", "position": "It disparages him as having unknown paternity or being born outside marriage.", "reasons": "Abū Saʿīd al-Ḍarīr takes waḥīdan as a second object of

Abū Ḥayyān raises the difficulty of using it as an insult and replies with the proper-name or uniquely evil readings."}, {"id": "74:11/q04/p7", "position": "His solitary beginning also points to his solitary return at resurrection.", "reasons": "Māwardī and Qurṭubī say he will be raised alone as he was created. {"id": "74:11/q05", "question": "What report explains the revelation about al-Walīd?", "turns_on": "The reports differ over whether the decisive setting was his private hearing followed by Abū Jahl's pressure or a Quraysh council preparing a public pilgrimage charge; recited passages and details also vary.", "positions": [{"id": "74:11/q05/p1", "position": "He was impressed by a recitation, but Abū Jahl pressed him into calling it transmitted magic.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and Ibn ʿAbbās say he softened and praised Qurʾan as sweet, radiant, fruitful, elevated, powerful and unlike poetry or human and jinn speech. Abū Jahl used Quraysh's fear that his conversion would attract the tribe, alleging he sought food or money from the Prophet or Abū Bakr. Al-Walīd rejected the allegation, reflected, then said it was inherited magic. Muqātil says the Prophet had recited Ghāfir 40:1–3 in the Sacred Mosque and repeated it when al-Walīd listened: God is sovereign and all-knowing, forgives repentant associators, severely punishes unrepentant shirk, is independent of unbelievers, affirms unity and receives all creatures in the hereafter. Al-Qummī names 41:13 instead. Al-Ḥākim authenticated the Ibn ʿAbbās report, also transmitted as ʿIkrima's mursal report; Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites al-Bayhaqī too. Durr preserves a variant in which al-Walīd said he would avoid Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and Muhammad. Muqātil says the accusation distressed the Prophet, whom 51:52 consoles by recalling earlier prophets accused of sorcery or madness. In Ibn Zayd's account, al-Walīd heard Muhammad reciting in prayer, called the speech sweet and heart-gripping, ruled out poetry and soothsaying, and suggested that it might be magic transmitted from earlier people."}, {"id": "74:11/q05/p2", "position": "At pilgrimage season, Quraysh sought one charge against Muhammad; al-Walīd rejected others and chose 'sorcerer' because the message divided families.", "reasons": "Ibn Hishām's Ibn Isḥāq report has Quraysh request a single story; al-Walīd rejects soothsayer, madman, poet and sorcerer as accurate, yet settles on sorcerer for the family-division allegation. Muqātil says he also rejected 'liar' because Muhammad was known as trustworthy, then pondered, grimaced (basara), changed color, and said magic. Muqātil also records his allegation that the magic came from Musaylima through Yāsar Abū Fukayha. Jishumī and Ibn ʿĀshūr give the council account; Mujāhid places it at Dār al-Nadwa, says Quraysh spread the verdict, and connects revelation through 74:25. Ibn Isḥāq calls him a contentious adversary. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ sets such claims among repeated Meccan allegations of human fabrication, borrowed ancient lore and dictated prior writings, citing 68:10–15, 68:44–47, 25:4–10, 17:87–96, 6:7–9, 6:25–26 and 34:43–45."}, {"id": "74:11/q05/p3", "position": "Muhammad invited al-Walīd to Islam; he delayed, reflected, frowned, turned away and called the message magic, whereupon he was consigned to Saqar.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk gives this sequence while identifying al-Walīd as the solitary man."}]}
{"id": "74:11/q06", "question": "How much of the passage was revealed about al-Walīd, and when?", "turns_on": "The extent assigned to the reported occasion and the chronology of al-Walīd's statement relative to the sūra's opening.", "positions": [{"id": "74:11/q06/p1", "position": "The verses from 74:11 through the threat of Saqar at 74:26 concern him.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd specifies the passage beginning here and ending at the threat of being cast into Saqar."}, {"id": "74:11/q06/p2", "position": "The revelation prompted by Quraysh's charge runs through 74:25.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's Dār al-Nadwa account says Quraysh spread the sorcery charge and the sūra was revealed through 74:25."}, {"id": "74:11/q06/p3", "position": "This verse and the following nineteen verses were revealed about him.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports abundant accounts for this extent.
